title: Controlled Forms
subtitle: Controlled inputs, form state, validation, and submission
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: HTML forms manage their own internal state (input.value). React's model is: state drives the UI. If the input has its own state that React can't see, React can't validate it, react to changes, or programmatically set its value.
whyItExists.solution: Controlled inputs: the input's value is driven by React state (value={state}) and React state is updated by onChange (onChange={e => setState(e.target.value)}). React is the single source of truth for the input's value.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any form where you need to validate, clear, prefill, or react to input changes as they happen. The default choice in React apps.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Uncontrolled inputs (ref-based) are OK for very simple cases where you only need the value at submit time (use useRef + FormData), or when integrating with non-React libraries.

explainModes.beginner: A controlled input has two things: value={someState} which shows the current state, and onChange={e => setSomeState(e.target.value)} which updates it when the user types. This means React knows the input's value at all times — unlike a plain HTML input that manages its own value.
explainModes.simple: Controlled: value + onChange pair. value without onChange = read-only (warning in console). Different inputs: text/number/email: e.target.value. Checkbox: e.target.checked. Select: e.target.value (of selected option). Form submission: onSubmit handler + e.preventDefault(). Validation: check state before allowing submit; show error messages based on state.
explainModes.standard: Form state pattern: one object for all fields: const [form, setForm] = useState({ name: '', email: '', age: '' }). Update one field: setForm(prev => ({ ...prev, [field]: value })). Validation state: const [errors, setErrors] = useState({}). Validate on blur (onBlur) or on submit. Touched fields: track which fields have been interacted with to avoid showing errors before the user touches a field.
explainModes.technical: react-hook-form: the industry-standard library for forms in React. It uses uncontrolled inputs internally (refs) for performance (no re-render on every keystroke), but exposes a controlled-like API: register() attaches the ref, handleSubmit wraps the submit handler, formState.errors gives validation errors. Zod or Yup: schema validation libraries that work with react-hook-form. TypeScript + react-hook-form: useForm<FormData>() is fully type-safe — form.register('name') knows 'name' is a key of FormData.
explainModes.deepDive: Performance: controlled forms re-render on every keystroke (every onChange). For complex forms with expensive renders, this matters. Solutions: (1) useReducer to batch updates, (2) react-hook-form with ref-based inputs (no re-render per keystroke), (3) split the form into components with React.memo. FormData API: the browser's native FormData reads all form inputs at submit time — useful for simple forms: onSubmit={e => { e.preventDefault(); const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(e.target)); }}. No state needed — but you can't validate as the user types.

questions.question: What makes an input 'controlled' in React?
options: Adding the controlled={true} attribute to the input element
Using an input inside a <form> element
Providing both value={state} and onChange={handler} — React state is the source of truth for the input's value
questions.explanation: A controlled input has its value driven by React state (value={someState}) and updates that state via onChange (onChange={e => setSomeState(e.target.value)}). React owns the value — you can't type into the input unless the onChange handler updates the state. An uncontrolled input has no value prop and manages its own value internally; you access it via a ref.

faq.q: Should I use a library like react-hook-form?
faq.a: For production apps with many forms, yes — react-hook-form dramatically reduces boilerplate, is performant (no re-render per keystroke), and integrates with validation schemas (Zod, Yup). For learning React or simple single-field scenarios, manual controlled inputs are fine and educational. Knowing how controlled inputs work helps you understand what libraries like react-hook-form are doing under the hood.
